questions.stem: Which form completes 'Nachdem wir gegessen ___, gingen wir spazieren.'?
questions.explanation: The meal came before the walk, which is told in the imperfect, so the earlier action goes in the pluperfect. 'Essen' takes 'haben', so the auxiliary is the imperfect 'hatten'.

questions.stem: Which form completes 'Nachdem sie nach Berlin gezogen ___, fand sie schnell neue Freunde.'?
questions.explanation: 'Ziehen' meaning to move house is a verb of motion and takes 'sein', so the pluperfect is 'war ... gezogen'. 'Ist' would be the perfect, which does not fit after a past main clause.

questions.stem: What does 'Als ich ankam, hatte der Film schon angefangen' mean?
options: When I arrive, the film will have started
When I arrived, the film was about to start
When I arrived, the film had already started
When I arrived, the film started straight away
questions.explanation: 'Hatte ... angefangen' is the pluperfect: the film started before the arrival. 'Schon' (already) supports that order of events.

questions.stem: Which word completes 'Ich hoffe, dass ich nächstes Jahr in Wien studieren ___.' ('will')?
questions.explanation: The future is 'werden' plus an infinitive. In a 'dass' clause the conjugated 'werde' goes to the very end, after the infinitive. 'Würde' would mean 'would', and 'wird' is the er/sie form.

questions.stem: In which sentence is 'werden' used to form the future tense?
options: Es wird am Abend langsam dunkel.
Das neue Haus wird gerade gebaut.
questions.explanation: Only the first has 'werden' with an infinitive ('abfahren'), the future. With an adjective or a number 'werden' means to become or turn; with a participle ('gebaut') it forms the passive.

questions.stem: Which form completes 'Als Kind ___ ich nicht allein in die Stadt fahren.' ('was not allowed to')?
questions.explanation: Modals drop their umlaut in the imperfect: 'dürfen' becomes 'durfte'. 'Dürfte', with the umlaut, is the subjunctive and means 'might'.

questions.stem: Which form completes 'Gestern ___ wir eine Stunde auf den Bus warten.' ('had to')?
questions.explanation: The imperfect of 'müssen' is 'musste', with no umlaut, and 'wir' takes '-en'. 'Müssten' is the subjunctive ('would have to').

questions.stem: Which form completes 'Meine Eltern ___ eigentlich nach Italien fahren, aber das Wetter war zu schlecht.' ('wanted to')?
questions.explanation: The subject 'meine Eltern' is plural, so the imperfect is 'wollten'. 'Wollte' is the ich/er/sie form, and 'wolltet' goes with 'ihr'.

questions.stem: What does 'Als Kind mochte ich keinen Spinat' mean?
options: As a child I could not eat spinach
As a child I would like no spinach
As a child I did not like spinach
As a child I was not allowed spinach
questions.explanation: 'Mochte' is the imperfect of 'mögen' (to like). 'Möchte', with the umlaut, means 'would like', so the umlaut changes the meaning.

questions.stem: What does 'Du musst das nicht essen' mean?
options: You do not have to eat that
questions.explanation: 'Nicht müssen' means there is no obligation. 'You must not' (a ban) is 'du darfst das nicht essen', a classic false match with English.

questions.stem: Which word completes 'Erinnerst du dich noch ___ unseren ersten Schultag?'?
questions.explanation: 'Sich erinnern an' plus the accusative means to remember. The accusative shows in 'unseren ersten Schultag'.

questions.stem: What is the difference between 'Ich freue mich auf die Party' and 'Ich freue mich über das Geschenk'?
options: The first describes a place; the second gives a reason
The first looks forward to it; the second is glad about something received
The first is formal; the second is used only among friends
The first is in the present; the second is in the past tense
questions.explanation: 'Sich freuen auf' is to look forward to something still to come. 'Sich freuen über' is to be pleased about something that has happened or is here now. Both sentences are present tense.

questions.stem: Which word completes 'Meine Mutter kümmert sich ___ meine kleine Schwester.'?
questions.explanation: 'Sich kümmern um' plus the accusative means to look after. English 'care for' tempts students to use 'für'.

questions.stem: Which word completes 'Ich kann mich nicht ___ das kalte Wetter gewöhnen.'?
questions.explanation: 'Sich gewöhnen an' plus the accusative means to get used to. The accusative shows in 'das kalte Wetter'.

questions.stem: Which word completes 'Darf ich dich ___ einen Gefallen bitten?'?
questions.explanation: 'Bitten um' means to ask for something. English 'ask for' tempts students to use 'für'; 'fragen nach' is to ask about.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: Ich habe keine Lust, heute ins Kino gehen.
Ich möchte heute gern ins Kino zu gehen.
Ich muss heute unbedingt ins Kino zu gehen.
Ich habe keine Lust, heute ins Kino zu gehen.
questions.explanation: Expressions such as 'Lust haben' are followed by 'zu' plus the infinitive. Modals such as 'möchte' and 'muss' take a bare infinitive, never 'zu'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly leaves out 'zu'?
options: Es ist schwer, jeden Tag früh aufstehen.
Er hat vergessen, die Tür abschließen.
questions.explanation: Verbs of motion such as 'gehen' take an infinitive without 'zu': 'schwimmen gehen'. The others need 'zu': 'aufzustehen', 'zu sprechen', 'abzuschließen'.

questions.stem: Which pair completes 'Er ging aus dem Haus, ___ sich ___ verabschieden.' ('without saying goodbye')?
questions.explanation: 'Ohne ... zu' plus the infinitive means without doing something. 'Um ... zu' means in order to, and 'statt ... zu' means instead of.

questions.stem: Which sentence means 'I hear him playing the piano'?
options: Ich höre, dass ihm Klavier spielt.
Ich höre ihn, Klavier zu spielen.
questions.explanation: Verbs of perception such as 'hören' and 'sehen' take an object plus a bare infinitive. The object of 'hören' is accusative, so 'ihn', not the dative 'ihm'.

questions.stem: Compare 'Das Museum wird um 18 Uhr geschlossen' and 'Das Museum ist montags geschlossen'. What does the second sentence describe?
options: The state the museum is in on Mondays
Someone closing the museum on Mondays
A closure that happened in the past
A closure planned for the future
questions.explanation: 'Sein' plus a participle is the statal passive: it describes a state (closed on Mondays). 'Werden' plus a participle is the actional passive: someone carries out the closing at six.

questions.stem: Which word completes 'Unsere Schule ___ im Jahr 1950 gegründet.' ('was founded')?
questions.explanation: The imperfect passive is 'wurde' plus the participle. 'Ist' alone would need 'worden' to make the perfect passive ('ist ... gegründet worden').

questions.stem: Which word completes 'Das Abendessen wird heute ___ meinem Vater gekocht.'?
questions.explanation: The person who does the action in a passive sentence is introduced by 'von' plus the dative. 'Mit' would give a tool or companion, not the cook.

questions.stem: Which form completes 'Die Einladungen ___ morgen verschickt.' ('are being sent')?
questions.explanation: 'Die Einladungen' is plural, so the present passive is 'werden' plus the participle. 'Wurden' is past and clashes with 'morgen'.

questions.stem: Which is the most polite way to order in a café?
options: Ich hätte gern einen Cappuccino, bitte.
questions.explanation: 'Ich hätte gern' (or 'ich möchte') is the polite way to order. 'Ich will' sounds demanding, and the 'du' imperative is too familiar for a waiter.

questions.stem: Which form completes 'Kinder, ___ mir bitte beim Tragen!' (helfen)?
questions.explanation: Speaking to several children uses the 'ihr' imperative, which is the 'ihr' form without the pronoun: 'helft'. 'Hilf' is for one person.

questions.stem: Which is the correct du-imperative in '___ bitte vorsichtig!' (fahren)?
questions.explanation: Verbs that change 'a' to 'ä' in the du form ('du fährst') drop the umlaut in the imperative: 'Fahr!'. Verbs that change 'e' to 'i' keep it ('Hilf!', 'Lies!'). 'Fahrt!' is for 'ihr'.

questions.stem: Which form completes '___ bitte leise, das Baby schläft!' (to one friend)?
questions.explanation: The du-imperative of 'sein' is irregular: 'Sei!'. 'Seid!' is said to several friends, and 'Seien Sie!' is the formal form.

questions.stem: Which sentence asks Frau Berger formally to close the window?
options: Sie machen bitte zu das Fenster, Frau Berger!
Machen Sie bitte das Fenster zu, Frau Berger!
Mach bitte das Fenster zu, Frau Berger!
Macht bitte das Fenster zu, Frau Berger!
questions.explanation: The formal imperative puts the verb first, then 'Sie', and the separable prefix 'zu' goes to the end. 'Mach' and 'macht' are the informal du and ihr forms.

questions.stem: Which form completes 'In unserer Straße gibt es ___ guten Bäcker.'?
questions.explanation: 'Es gibt' is always followed by the accusative, so masculine 'ein' becomes 'einen'.

questions.stem: Which word completes 'Wie ___ dir deine neue Schule?' ('How do you like ...')?
questions.explanation: With 'gefallen' the thing liked is the subject and the person is dative ('dir'). The subject 'deine neue Schule' is singular, so the verb is 'gefällt'. 'Magst' would need 'du' as the subject.
